rv.q: If you’re fond of laughing, “Shucked” is the best new musical of the Broadway season so far.
With its exuberance, heart and non-stop yucks, 'Shucked' is the surprise delight of the season.
When all’s said and done, Shucked is exactly as much fun as you’ll let it be.
And snorts, giggles and rolled eyes are what it delivers.
The proof is in the (corn) pudding and the fact that everyone around you does end up laughing.
The thing is defiantly irreducible, because its aims are simple and direct.
This corny musical about corn farmers is both aggressively silly and surprisingly sweet.
With its gentle digs at small-town closed-mindedness, it might end up working best in the blue-voting urban precincts of red states.
The musical's appeal lies in its commitment to the ridiculous, its willingness to lean into the corniest possible jokes about corn and small-town life.
Embrace each grain of fun and you’ll have an amazing night on Broadway.
There’s no law that states musical comedy can’t have deep feels, but the proportions are a little off.
About one-third of the jokes land — and most (like Peanut’s) come out of nowhere, having nothing to do with the story or its characters.
Like Gordy, the audience may have difficulty extracting the gems from the corn.
The answers are: yes, not really and kind of, depending heavily on your taste for, surprise surprise, corniness (and dad jokes).
Before you know it, you're gorged to satisfaction on a big, tasty bag of Broadway puff.
For all the show’s silly jackass humor, it’s carried by a top-notch score that manages to combine a solid country sound with classic Broadway appeal.
As long as New York audiences—many themselves from rural places—don’t mind too much hick in their shtick, Shucked should keep Broadway laughing till the cows come home.
It’s all about laughs, and it delivers – honest to cob.

Go see Shucked, you’ll laugh, a lot, at the wonderful wit, you’ll join in the jubilation as the whole audience elatedly exclaims together as the corn visibly comes back to life, and you’ll maybe even shed a tear.
Shucked is about as quick and easy a good time can be had on Broadway: accessible, unpretentious and, I’ll be damned, a whole lot of fun.
In Shucked (Nederlander Theatre, booking to Sept 3), they are deliciously relentless.
It will cause you to have a big smile on your face – and nothing in your teeth – for two hours.
I'd be lying if I didn't admit to laughing a good seventy-five percent of the time.
Let’s just go with an endearing, soil-kicking “Aw, shucks!”

The musical, featuring a book by Robert Horn (Tootsie) and songs by Nashville veterans Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally, emerges as one of the brightest surprises of the spring season, delivering more hilarious gags per minute than any show since The Book of Mormon.

Add in an appealing, occasionally rowdy country-inflected score by the Grammy-winning songwriting team of Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally, and you've got yourself a show that is both whimsically hokey and welcoming as an old friend.
If you're considering buying tickets to Broadway's newest musical comedy, 'Shucked' — and I recommend that you do
Much like the experience of eating corn, Shucked is kind of great.
Even if you’re not in the mood for some feel-good sentiment, as a laugh-out-loud crowd-pleaser, ‘Shucked’ is a shucking good time.

Scott Pask’s set is a big wooden barn that practically gives you splinters when you look at it, and three-time Tony-winning director Jack O’Brien (Hairspray) and choreographer Sarah O’Gleby keep things moving so you don’t stop and ponder too much about plot developments dealing with who kissed whom, not to mention a dumb bit about the dual sets ...

One could try to read into it as a parable of community, commitment, tolerance, and so on, but “Shucked” is really just a lightweight and laborious attempt at resurrecting old-fashioned musical comedy with a country flavor and corn as high as an elephant’s eye.
This constant switching of gears between the songs and the joke-filled dialogue slows down the narrative, making “Shucked” seem a lot longer than its two and twenty minutes with intermission.
Otherwise, you might find yourself bored or exasperated.

Shucked is the theatrical version of the latter, a solidly second-rate effort whose bonhomie might even make it ribbon-worthy come awards time thanks to the current Broadway season’s underwhelming original output (Bad Cinderella, indeed).
Most importantly, it is loads of fun.
Shucked weaves together a thoroughly enjoyable theatrical experience, juxtaposing immature puns with songs that actually have a lot to say.
If they happen to be looking for a tight, well written Broadway musical with substance and pay full price for a ticket, they may feel they've been 'Shucked.'
Shucked is unable to till the potentially fertile premise, however ridiculous, instead relying on Horn’s automated joke harvester.

cn.t: Critics find this aggressively corny musical comedy a surprisingly enjoyable guilty pleasure, praising its relentless barrage of puns and catchy country score while noting the humor's mileage varies wildly by taste.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
